subject: biology-hl
topicLabel: B2.1 — Membranes & membrane transport (Form & function — cells)

cards.back: Has a hydrophilic part and a hydrophobic part, like a phospholipid: phosphate head attracted to water, two fatty-acid tails repelled by it.

cards.front: Why do phospholipids form a bilayer in water?
cards.back: Heads face the water on both sides and the tails cluster together in the middle, away from water. This happens spontaneously.

cards.front: What can and can't cross the hydrophobic core of the bilayer easily?
cards.back: Small non-polar molecules cross easily (O₂, CO₂). Ions, large or polar molecules (glucose, amino acids, proteins) barely cross, so the bilayer acts as a barrier.
Passive net movement of particles down a concentration gradient directly between phospholipids. No protein, no ATP. Example: O₂ and CO₂.
Integral: embedded in the bilayer, often spanning it (transmembrane). Peripheral: attached to one surface only, to lipid heads or integral proteins.
Net movement of water across a partially permeable membrane from lower to higher solute concentration (higher to lower water potential).
Channel protein specific for water; greatly increases a membrane's permeability to water.

cards.front: How do channel proteins give facilitated diffusion its selectivity?
cards.back: Each channel has a pore of a particular diameter with a charged lining, so only specific ions or molecules pass. Movement is passive, down the gradient; many channels are gated.
A pump uses energy from ATP to change shape and moves specific particles AGAINST their gradient (active transport). A channel only allows passive movement down the gradient.

cards.front: Which membrane transport mechanisms are selective?
cards.back: Facilitated diffusion and active transport (they depend on specific proteins). Simple diffusion is not selective: it depends only on size and polarity.

cards.front: Glycoproteins and glycolipids: where and why?
cards.back: Carbohydrate chains on the outer (extracellular) face only. Roles: cell–cell recognition (e.g. ABO blood-group antigens) and cell adhesion.

cards.front: Fluid mosaic model: what must the diagram show?
cards.back: Phospholipid bilayer; integral and peripheral proteins; glycoproteins with carbohydrate facing out; cholesterol among the tails; hydrophilic and hydrophobic regions labelled.

cards.front: AHL: How does fatty-acid saturation affect membrane fluidity?
cards.back: Unsaturated (cis double bonds) tails are kinked and pack loosely: more fluid at low temperature. Saturated tails pack tightly: more rigid. Cold-water ectotherms have more unsaturated fatty acids in their membranes.

cards.front: AHL: Role of cholesterol in animal membranes
cards.back: A fluidity buffer: it restrains phospholipid movement when warm (less fluid) and stops the tails packing tightly when cold (prevents stiffening).

cards.front: AHL: Endocytosis and exocytosis, one example each
cards.back: Both rely on membrane fluidity. Endocytosis: a phagocyte engulfing a bacterium. Exocytosis: pancreatic cells secreting digestive enzymes, or neurotransmitter release at a synapse.

cards.front: AHL: Neurotransmitter-gated vs voltage-gated channels, one example each
cards.back: Neurotransmitter-gated: nicotinic acetylcholine receptor opens when acetylcholine binds, letting Na⁺ in. Voltage-gated: Na⁺ and K⁺ channels in axons open when the membrane potential changes.
Per ATP: 3 Na⁺ pumped out, 2 K⁺ pumped in, both against their gradients. Net loss of positive charge helps set the negative resting potential.

cards.front: AHL: Sodium-dependent glucose cotransport — why 'indirect' active transport?
cards.back: The cotransporter uses no ATP. Na⁺ moves in down the gradient made by the Na⁺/K⁺ pump and carries glucose in against its gradient. Small intestine and nephron (glucose reabsorption).
Membrane proteins that bind neighbouring cells together; different CAMs form different types of cell–cell junction.
